title: The Paperwork

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA has already filed your paperwork! She also signed you up for the colony newsletter. You're welcome!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has read the Terms and Conditions. All 4,000 pages. He advises against departure. He has filed the paperwork anyway.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has classified the departure paperwork as a bureaucratic threat. He has filed it under protest.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that your departure is sponsored by ColonyStart™ — 'Making New Worlds Feel Like Obligation Since 2340!'
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has reviewed the waiver. It's comprehensive. Impressively so, actually. Almost as if they expect things to go wrong. But I'm sure that's just legal being thorough.

body:
You are cleared to leave Earth orbit. There is paperwork.

The colony authority requires a signed acknowledgment that you understand the risks, a waiver of liability for 'unforeseen botanical failure,' and a form confirming you have read the Terms and Conditions.

You have not read the Terms and Conditions.

The ship computer files these automatically. It notes that your crop is already growing. It does not say 'good luck' because it is a computer.

It does say 'departure confirmed' in a way that almost sounds like good luck.

outcome.narrative: You signed. The computer noted your reading speed was 'impressive.' Nobody comments.

choices.text: Actually read the Terms and Conditions

outcome.narrative: You read them. Section 47, paragraph 3: 'The colony authority is not responsible for emotional attachment to vegetation.' You are less optimistic now. You are better informed. These are not the same thing.

choices.text: Ask the ship computer to summarize

outcome.narrative: The computer summarizes: 'You are responsible for everything. The colony authority is responsible for nothing. Your crop is legally classified as cargo. You may not agree with this classification. This does not change the classification.'

alt_bodies:
Earth orbit, departure window open, and a stack of forms on the console.

The colony authority needs your signature on a risk acknowledgment, a liability waiver covering 'unforeseen botanical failure,' and a declaration that you have read the Terms and Conditions.

You have not read the Terms and Conditions. Nobody has read the Terms and Conditions.

The ship computer files everything else on your behalf and notes that the crop is already growing. It is a computer, so it does not wish you luck. It says 'departure confirmed' with what might, in a person, be a small smile.

The last thing Earth sends you is paperwork.

It arrives on the console while you wait for undocking clearance: a form acknowledging the risks, a waiver releasing the colony authority from 'unforeseen botanical failure', and a box to tick confirming you have read the Terms and Conditions. The Terms and Conditions are attached. They are longer than the route.

The ship computer processes the rest automatically and reports that the crop is already growing. It doesn't say good luck. It isn't built to. It does say 'departure confirmed', and lingers on it a moment longer than it needs to.

title: Departure Protocol

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA reports all systems green! Some of them are actually green! The rest are close enough!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has completed the pre-launch checklist. Everything is technically functional. He emphasizes 'technically.'
ai_flavor.rex: REX has completed threat assessment of the departure corridor. Threat level: low. He seems disappointed.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP reminds you that your departure window is brought to you by QuickLaunch™ — 'Because Time Is Money, Especially Yours.'
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY notes the pre-launch checklist is complete. She also notes that the checklist doesn't cover most of the things that actually go wrong. But sure, the checklist is done.

body:
The ship computer runs through a pre-launch checklist. Hull integrity: acceptable. Fuel reserves: adequate. Crew: accounted for. Crop: growing.

Every item is technically fine. The tone of the computer's voice suggests 'technically fine' is doing a lot of heavy lifting.

Earth is about to be behind you. The computer notes the departure time, the destination, and the estimated travel duration. There was a third number it calculated. It does not share it.

choices.text: Check the crop one last time before departure

outcome.narrative: The crop is fine. You knew it was fine. Checking it made you feel better. The ship computer logs this as 'pre-departure botanical anxiety' which it assures you is common.

choices.text: Review the route on the chart

outcome.narrative: The route looks straightforward. The chart has been updated recently. Some of the annotations are helpful. Some are just the word 'no' written next to a waypoint. You do not investigate this.
Departure confirmed. The stars don't move. You do.

alt_bodies:
The ship computer reads out the pre-launch checklist. Hull integrity: acceptable. Fuel reserves: adequate. Crew: accounted for. Crop: growing.

Nothing on the list is wrong. Nothing on the list is right, either, exactly. The computer delivers each item in the tone of a doctor saying 'well, it's not nothing.'

Earth is about to drop away behind you. The computer logs the time of departure, the destination and the expected length of the trip. It worked out one more figure. It keeps that one to itself.

Checklist. Hull integrity: acceptable. Fuel reserves: adequate. Crew: accounted for. Crop: growing.

The ship computer reads each line, ticks it and moves on, and somehow the ticks read less like approval than like a reluctant signature. Acceptable. Adequate. The words are carrying more than their share.

Below the station, Earth turns, huge and close, for the last time. The computer records the departure time, the destination and the journey estimate, and then one more calculation, which it files somewhere you can't read.

title: Porch Lights

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA is counting the lights! She has reached a very large number and started again! Every single one of them is for US!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has matched the blinking against the census. Participation is unusually high. He suspects somebody declared a holiday. He finds he does not mind.
ai_flavor.rex: REX reads the pattern as unauthorised signalling across a whole continent. He has decided not to report it. He has decided this twice.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes the electricity for this send-off is being paid for by the people down there! The most generous sponsorship CHIP has ever seen! CHIP is moved! CHIP is checking whether it's tax-deductible!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says the ship can wait an orbit for them. They waited a lot longer than that for the ship.

body:
Undocked and waiting on the departure window, the ship swings across the night side of Earth.

Somebody down there organised it. Nobody aboard knows who. As the ship passes over, the dark below starts to blink: porch lights, headlights, phone screens held up on rooftops, whole streets switching off and on in a slow ripple that follows your ground track across a continent.

It is the oldest send-off there is, done with every light they have. The departure burn is queued. The ship computer points out, unprompted, that it could also wait for another pass.

outcome.narrative: You blink the running lights in the only pattern anyone aboard knows, which turns out to be the one for help. Below, a whole city goes dark, then bright, then dark again, which everyone decides means 'you're welcome.' The burn fires on schedule.

choices.text: Hold the burn for another pass

outcome.narrative: You stay up for another orbit and the lights are waiting, brighter, as if word got round. The correction burn afterwards costs fuel the plan didn't have in it. Nobody aboard will ever count that fuel as wasted, and the ship computer, for once, does not try.

choices.text: Burn on the mark — the window won't wait

outcome.narrative: You burn on the exact second the window opens, the cheapest departure the ship will ever make. The lights carry on blinking behind you on the rear camera, smaller and smaller, until they are just the night side again. The crew watches the screen until there is nothing left to watch.

title: The Hive

ai_flavor.aria: BEES! ARIA has named every one of them! It took a while! Most of them are called Gary!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has checked the manifest. The bees are not on it. Neither, he observes, is the forklift driver's sense of responsibility.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has assessed the hive. Several thousand armed units, no command structure he can identify, total loyalty. He respects them. He is staying on the bridge.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that pollination is a premium agricultural service! Normally billed by the hour! Per bee! CHIP is doing the maths and getting very excited!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says they'll be calmer if nobody shouts. She's turned the growbay lamps down a little. They've settled on the warm side.

body:
While the ship waits on the departure burn, the growbay sensors report an unregistered life form. Several thousand of them.

They are bees. A whole hive, in a crate stencilled POLLINATION SERVICES — HANDLE WITH CONFIDENCE, meant for the colony ship in the next bay and loaded onto yours by a forklift driver who has, by now, gone home. The bees have already found the {crop.name}. They seem to approve of it.

The departure dock is still right there. Traffic control would like to know, on an open channel, why you are calling about bees.

choices.text: Keep them — the crop could use the help

outcome.narrative: You keep the bees. They need feeding, which means the galley's sugar and a good part of the dried fruit go into a syrup tray by the lamps. In return they work the crop from first watch to last, and it fills out in a way no hand-brush ever managed.

You re-dock, which costs fuel and an apologetic call to traffic control. The other ship's botanist meets you at the dock, takes the crate in both arms like a returned child, and makes the whole crew promise to visit. The second departure is a lot more cheerful than the first.

choices.text: Hold for the dock's courier and charge for it

outcome.narrative: You hold position while the other ship sends a courier drone for its bees, and you invoice them for 'bee husbandry, in transit.' They pay, mostly to stop the conversation. The growbay is very quiet afterwards. Somebody misses them already and won't say so.

science_link.text: The ship computer files a reference beside the hive's entry: honeybees have flown in space before, and learned to build comb without gravity, eventually.
science_link.label: Animals in space

title: The Sponsor

ai_flavor.aria: We have a MASCOT! ARIA has always wanted a mascot! ARIA is going to give the oat a name and a backstory!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has read the contract. One clause grants the cereal company the naming rights to anything the ship discovers. He recommends discovering nothing.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has run the oat through target recognition. It came back friendly. He does not trust anything that smiles that widely.
ai_flavor.chip: CRUNCHEE-O'S™! CHIP has waited his whole life for this! CHIP also has a rival cereal on the other line! CHIP can start a bidding war!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY points out the money is real and the paint comes off eventually. Space is very good at taking paint off. It just isn't quick about it.

body:
A shuttle catches up with the ship before the first burn, which should not be possible, and docks without asking, which should not be allowed.

Out steps a man in a very good suit and a pressure helmet with a logo on it. He represents CRUNCHEE-O'S, the breakfast cereal that is, he says, going further. He would like the ship to go further too, with the CRUNCHEE-O'S mascot painted down both sides of the hull: a cheerful cartoon oat with its arms flung wide.

He has a contract. He has a cheque. He has a drone outside that has already painted one arm.

outcome.narrative: You sign. The drone finishes the oat in an afternoon, and from then on the ship arrives everywhere as a giant smiling breakfast cereal. The money is very welcome. The crew learns to answer hails with a straight face, more or less.

You decline. The man takes it well, shakes everyone's hand, and leaves a crate of free samples nobody eats. The drone leaves too, without removing the arm it already painted. The ship flies on with a single cartoon arm on its flank, waving at the dark, and the crew grows fond of it.

{crew.diplomat} takes the man into the galley for an hour. When they come out, the oat is going on the underside of the hull, where only the colony will see it, and the fee has somehow gone up, on the grounds of exclusivity. The man looks pleased and slightly confused. That is usually how it goes.
